narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year performance in law school had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class after the first year is much weaker than the average student who was accepted, who typically ranked around the 6th decile. Your third-year class ranking added further weight in the same direction, placing you in the second decile compared with an average of nearly the sixth decile among accepted applicants.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.40 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your early law-school performance.

Taken together, the model concluded that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. To improve your chances next time, focus on strengthening your academic record in law school, particularly by raising your class ranking in the early years. Consider targeted bar-preparation resources or additional coursework that builds the exact skills tested on the exam. Reapply once you can demonstrate clearer evidence that you are likely to pass on the first attempt.
